headline: The Emergency Medicine Foundation
threshold: By Lesson 10, you can greet ER patients, give vital signs in numbers, describe a patient with ser and estar, ask basic history questions, give simple polite commands and get help in Spanish, and start Emergency Medicine Lesson 1.

lessons.title: Sounds and Greetings
lessons.objective: Pronounce Spanish ER words clearly and greet patients and staff politely.
lessons.focus: The five vowels, ch, j, ll, rr and the written accent; greetings for patients and staff

words.note: Stress the accent: MÉ-di-co. A woman is la médica or la doctora.
A man is el enfermero.
A woman is la paciente; the word does not change.
Five pure vowels: ca-BE-za; z sounds like s in Latin America.
ch sounds like the ch in church.
j sounds like a strong English h: O-ho.
ll sounds like English y: ca-MI-ya.
An r at the start of a word is rolled like rr; stress the í.
The accent marks the stressed syllable: co-ra-ZÓN.
g before e or i sounds like English h: ur-HEN-sias.

words.es: Buenos días, soy el doctor Ramírez.
words.note: A woman says soy la doctora.
Formal usted form; use it with patients.
Formal; use it with patients and families.
Buenas noches means both good evening and good night.

lessons.speaking: Greet a patient on a stretcher, say your name and that you are the doctor, and ask the patient's name.

lessons.title: Numbers, Time and Measurements
lessons.objective: Say numbers, clock time, basic vital signs and weights to ER staff.
lessons.focus: Numbers 0 to 1,000, clock time, and vital signs, pounds, degrees, mg and mL with de

words.note: In speech, often just la presión.
US hospitals usually give temperature in Fahrenheit.
Written mg; say miligramos aloud.
Written mL; say mililitros aloud.
Patients in the US usually give their weight in pounds.
Measurements take de: es de 110.
Use es la for 1 o'clock: es la 1.
hace + time = ago.

lessons.speaking: Read a patient's pulse, blood pressure and temperature to a nurse, and say what time the pain started.

lessons.title: Ser and Estar
lessons.objective: Say who a patient or staff member is and how or where a patient is, using ser and estar.
lessons.focus: ser for what someone is, estar for a patient's condition or location

words.note: Same form for a man or a woman.
estar grave: to be seriously ill or injured.
Same form for a man or a woman.
mareada for a woman.
pálida for a woman.
despierta for a woman.
herida for a woman.
Means a relative; plural los familiares.
estar: a condition that can change.

words.es: Ella es la enfermera a cargo.
words.note: ser: who someone is.
Ask a woman ¿Está mareada?

words.es: La paciente está en el cuarto 4.
words.note: estar for location.

lessons.speaking: Tell the charge nurse whether your patient is stable, awake, dizzy or pale, and which room the patient is in.

lessons.title: Have, There Is, Need and Want
lessons.objective: Ask about fever, allergies and symptoms, and say what you need and what must be done.
lessons.focus: tener, hay, necesitar, querer and hay que + infinitive for symptoms and needs

words.note: Patients also say el medicamento or las pastillas.
In Mexico, el suero is the everyday word for IV fluids.
Patients often say tengo vómito or estoy vomitando.
Patients may also say no puedo respirar.

words.en: Are you allergic to any medicine?
Do you have a fever or a cough?
There is blood on the stretcher.
words.note: hay: there is / there are.

words.es: Necesito una silla de ruedas, por favor.

words.en: Do you want to call your family?
We need to take the vital signs.
words.es: Hay que tomar los signos vitales.
words.note: hay que + infinitive: something must be done.

lessons.speaking: Ask a patient about fever, cough and allergies, then tell a nurse what you need for the patient.

lessons.title: Go, Do and Can
lessons.objective: Say your next steps and the tests you will order, and ask what a patient can do.
lessons.focus: ir, ir a + infinitive for next steps, hacer, and poder for what a patient can do

words.note: The usual word for a CT scan in Mexico.

words.en: I'm going to examine your chest.
words.note: ir a + infinitive: a plan or the next step.

words.en: We're going to do a CT scan.
Can you go to the restroom by yourself?
words.note: Ask a woman ¿Puede ir al baño sola?

words.en: The nurse is going to take the sample to the lab.
words.es: La enfermera va a llevar la muestra al laboratorio.
words.note: a + el = al.

words.en: Your family can wait in the waiting room.
words.es: Su familia puede esperar en la sala de espera.

lessons.speaking: Tell a patient which tests you are going to do, and ask whether the patient can walk to the restroom.

lessons.title: Present Tense
lessons.objective: Use present-tense verbs to ask patients about habits and tell staff what you do.
lessons.focus: Present tense of regular -ar, -er, -ir verbs: yo, tú, usted, nosotros, ellos

words.note: Patients also say la panza (informal).
Also means doll; on the body it is the wrist.

words.en: I write the order and you call the lab.
words.es: Yo escribo la orden y tú llamas al laboratorio.
words.note: tú between coworkers; use usted with patients.

words.en: Do you smoke or drink alcohol?
We are checking the leg now.

words.note: ellos form: -ar verbs end in -an.
Ask a man ¿Usted vive solo?

lessons.speaking: Ask a patient if they smoke, drink alcohol or live alone, then tell a nurse which body part you are checking.

lessons.title: Questions
lessons.objective: Ask basic ER questions about pain, time, people, place and identity.
lessons.focus: Question words: qué, quién, dónde, cuándo, cuánto, cómo, por qué, cuál

words.note: For counting use cuántos or cuántas: ¿cuántas pastillas?
The answer uses porque, one word with no accent.
Use cuál es for a name, number or date.
le duele: it hurts you (formal).

words.en: What is your date of birth?
words.note: Confirm identity with full name and date of birth.

lessons.speaking: Ask a patient where it hurts, when the pain started, who came with them, and their date of birth.

lessons.title: No, Never and How Much
lessons.objective: Say no, never, nobody and not yet, and ask for more, less or another item in the ER.
lessons.focus: no, nunca, nadie, nada, todavía no, más, menos and otro

words.note: After a verb, add no: no hay nadie.
After a verb, add no: no come nada.
otra before feminine nouns: otra cobija. Never say un otro.
Mexican usage; also la manta.

words.en: You can't eat anything for now.
words.es: No puede comer nada por ahora.

words.en: Nobody is with the patient in room 2.
words.es: Nadie está con el paciente del cuarto 2.

words.en: Does it hurt more or less now?
words.es: ¿Ahora le duele más o le duele menos?

words.en: I need another blanket for the patient.
words.es: Necesito otra cobija para la paciente.

words.en: He never takes medicine, according to his wife.
words.es: Él nunca toma medicinas, según su esposa.

lessons.speaking: Tell a nurse the results aren't back yet, that nobody is with a patient, and that you need another blanket.

lessons.title: Polite Requests and Commands
lessons.objective: Ask patients politely to do simple exam steps with ¿Puede…? and usted commands.
lessons.focus: ¿Puede…? + infinitive and usted commands for simple exam steps

words.note: Ends in -o but is feminine: la mano.

words.en: Can you put on the gown, please?
words.note: ¿Puede…? + infinitive is a polite request.

words.en: Open your mouth and stick out your tongue.
words.es: Abra la boca y saque la lengua.

words.note: Usted command: apretar becomes apriete.

words.en: Lie down on your left side.

lessons.speaking: Ask a patient politely to put on the gown, open their mouth, take a deep breath and squeeze your fingers.

lessons.title: Words You Already Know and Getting Help
lessons.objective: Recognize ER cognates and use survival phrases to get help when you don't understand.
lessons.focus: Cognates ending in -ción, -dad and -ente; survival phrases for getting help

words.note: Words ending in -ción are feminine and match English -tion.
Doctors also say la cirugía.
Words ending in -dad are feminine and often match English -ty.
A woman is la residente.
A woman is la intérprete.
-ente adjectives do not change for a woman.

words.en: Can you repeat it more slowly, please?
I'm going to call an interpreter.
words.es: Voy a llamar a un intérprete.
words.note: Use the personal a before a person: llamar a un intérprete.

words.en: How do you say this in Spanish?

lessons.speaking: Tell a patient you speak a little Spanish, ask them to repeat more slowly, and say you will call an interpreter.
